title: Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer Risk Factors Identified
summary: A California population-based nested case-control study linked birth records and cancer registries (1988–2021) for 1,221 early-onset colorectal cancer cases and 61,050 controls. Male sex and Hispanic ethnicity were associated with increased risk, while having a foreign-born mother was protective. Among females, higher birthweight and paternal age ≥35 were linked to elevated risk. No associations were found for gestational age, birth order, delivery mode, plurality, maternal age, education, or pregnancy complications.
content:
This site is intended for healthcare professionals

MALE sex and Hispanic ethnicity increase early-onset colorectal cancer risk, while foreign maternal birthplace provides protection. In a large population-based nested case-control study from the California Linkage Study of Early-Onset Cancers, investigators evaluated statewide birth records matched with cancer registry data from 1988 through 2021. The investigation encompassed 1,221 individuals diagnosed with first primary early-onset colorectal cancer between ages 0 and 39 years, along with 61,050 birth-year matched control subjects without cancer diagnoses. Researchers performed multivariable logistic regression to elucidate how demographic, birth, and parental characteristics influence early malignancy.

Fully adjusted statistical models revealed distinct demographic disparities in cancer risk. Males demonstrated a 34 percent increased risk of developing early-onset colorectal cancer compared with females. Additionally, Hispanic ethnicity was associated with a 43 percent higher risk compared to non-Hispanic White individuals. Stratified analyses showed elevated risk among Hispanic males and females alike. Conversely, offspring born to foreign-born mothers exhibited a 15 percent lower overall risk of developing early-onset disease, an effect particularly pronounced among male offspring who experienced a 21 percent risk reduction.

Sex-stratified evaluations demonstrated that specific biological and developmental variables selectively alter early-onset colorectal cancer risk factors. Among female offspring, each 500-gram increase in birthweight was associated with a 10 percent increase in cancer risk. Furthermore, females born to fathers aged 35 years or older faced a 56 percent elevated risk of developing colorectal cancer compared to those with younger fathers. Among young adults aged 20 to 39 years, higher birthweight also correlated with a 5 percent risk increase per 500-gram increment.

No statistically significant associations were identified for gestational age, birth order, delivery mode, birth plurality, maternal age, maternal education, or maternal pregnancy complications. Clinical management of early-onset disease requires ongoing investigation into early environmental exposures, maternal metabolic health, and paternal age mechanisms. Understanding how these early-life influences shape early-onset colorectal cancer risk factors will assist clinicians in recognizing subtle predispositions and informing future screening considerations.

Reference

Siddique S et al. Demographic, birth, parental characteristics, and the risk of early-onset colorectal cancer: A population-based nested case-control study in California. Cancer. 2026;e70458. doi:10.1002/cncr.70458

## Study overview

Male sex and Hispanic ethnicity increase early-onset colorectal cancer risk, while foreign maternal birthplace provides protection. In a large population-based nested case-control study from the California Linkage Study of Early-Onset Cancers, investigators evaluated statewide birth records matched with cancer registry data from 1988 through 2021. The investigation encompassed 1,221 individuals diagnosed with first primary early-onset colorectal cancer between ages 0 and 39 years, along with 61,050 birth-year matched control subjects without cancer diagnoses. Researchers performed multivariable logistic regression to elucidate how demographic, birth, and parental characteristics influence early malignancy.

## Key findings

Fully adjusted statistical models revealed distinct demographic disparities in cancer risk:

- Males demonstrated a 34 percent increased risk of developing early-onset colorectal cancer compared with females.
- Hispanic ethnicity was associated with a 43 percent higher risk compared to non-Hispanic White individuals.
- Offspring born to foreign-born mothers exhibited a 15 percent lower overall risk of developing early-onset disease, an effect particularly pronounced among male offspring who experienced a 21 percent risk reduction.

## Sex-stratified and age-stratified results

Sex-stratified evaluations demonstrated that specific biological and developmental variables selectively alter early-onset colorectal cancer risk factors:

- Among female offspring:
  - Each 500-gram increase in birthweight was associated with a 10 percent increase in cancer risk.
  - Females born to fathers aged 35 years or older faced a 56 percent elevated risk of developing colorectal cancer compared to those with younger fathers.
- Among young adults aged 20 to 39 years:
  - Higher birthweight correlated with a 5 percent risk increase per 500-gram increment.

## Non-significant associations

No statistically significant associations were identified for:

- Gestational age
- Birth order
- Delivery mode
- Birth plurality
- Maternal age
- Maternal education
- Maternal pregnancy complications

## Clinical implications

Clinical management of early-onset disease requires ongoing investigation into early environmental exposures, maternal metabolic health, and paternal age mechanisms. Understanding how these early-life influences shape early-onset colorectal cancer risk factors will assist clinicians in recognizing subtle predispositions and informing future screening considerations.
